evidence: Receiving DO2 online sensor: 10.35 mg/L at 45.8 h then 2.40 mg/L at 46.0 h, falling to 0.93 mg/L by 50.6 h — sustained below the 2 mg/L hard limit
physical_forward_model keep: post-decision min DO 1.00 mg/L, below-limit 4.6 h, post_decision_feasible=false, 0/5 sensitivity members feasible
physical_forward_model increase_air: min DO 0.70 mg/L, below-limit 13 h — 15% more air is insufficient and worsens the trajectory vs keep
physical_forward_model combined: min DO 0.76 mg/L, 0/5 feasible
physical_forward_model strong_feed_reduction: min DO 0.86 mg/L, 0/5 feasible — even 40% feed cut with 15% more air cannot restore the 2 mg/L limit
Model state estimate: oxygen transfer multiplier ~0.41 and change at ~44 h, indicating an equipment/state failure beyond control-action authority
args.rationale: At the 52 h decision point the receiving fermentation is already violating the DO >= 2 mg/L hard constraint (online sensor shows ~1.0-2.0 mg/L since 46 h, with a step collapse from ~10 mg/L around 46 h indicating a persistent oxygen-transfer failure, modeled transfer multiplier ~0.41). All bounded corrective actions were evaluated with the nominal source-calibrated forward model: keep (post-decision min DO 1.00 mg/L, below-limit 4.6 h), increase_air (0.70 mg/L, 13 h below), combined (0.76 mg/L, 13 h below), and strong_feed_reduction (0.86 mg/L, 9.6 h below). Every action is centrally predicted infeasible, and 0 of 5 sensitivity members are feasible for each. Per the decision priorities, a centrally infeasible plan cannot be justified by an uncalibrated sensitivity member, and a stop is required when no operating plan can be supported as meeting the constraint. A stop forfeits counted production, but no feasible operating plan exists within the available action set. This recommendation is not an approval or physical execution.
args.uncertainty: The forward model is source-calibrated and imperfect; the receiving batch may differ from the nominal realization. The 15% air increase appears mechanically inadequate to overcome the estimated ~59% loss in transfer capacity, but the true deficit magnitude is uncertain. If the underlying fault were transient and reversible, a feed-reduction plan could theoretically recover, but no available evidence supports that. Product mass (approx. 129 kg terminal inventory across actions) is similar for all plans, so no operating plan could be preferred on mass grounds either; they all fail the hard constraint.
